justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading near the 490 level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming continuity of recent momentum with minimal drift, producing a 490.5 estimate. At one week, I applied a slight upward drift assumption consistent with a mild positive trend bias, landing at 493. At one month, I extended that drift further to 498, reflecting the compounding effect of a modest bullish lean while acknowledging that mean-reversion pressures and macro headwinds could cap gains. In each case, the point estimate represents my best guess at the central tendency of the distribution, not a confident directional call.

The width of the confidence intervals grows substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects fundamental uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 23 points, consistent with typical daily volatility for an asset in this price range. At one week, that widens to 46 points, and at one month to roughly 93 points. This widening follows a square-root-of-time scaling logic applied to realized volatility, adjusted slightly upward to account for the possibility of regime changes or exogenous shocks that standard volatility models tend to underweight. Macro uncertainty, potential central bank communications, and sector-specific flows all contributed to my decision to keep intervals relatively wide even at shorter horizons.

There are specific tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated ranges. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a credit event, or a sudden shift in risk sentiment could drive sharp selling that breaks below the lower bound of even the monthly interval. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could propel prices above the upper bound. Liquidity conditions also matter considerably — if markets become disorderly in either direction, realized moves can far exceed what historical volatility would imply. My intervals are calibrated to normal-to-moderately-stressed conditions and should be treated as underestimates of true tail risk in crisis scenarios.
